client: I've been having a really hard time at family get-togethers since my grandmother passed away six months ago. Everyone else seems to be moving on and laughing and talking like normal, but I just feel completely out of place, like I'm watching it all through a glass wall. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem isn't really in my head — she's just gone, and nothing can fix that.
therapist: What you're describing — that sense of being separated from everyone else by an invisible wall — sounds incredibly lonely, and you're right that nothing can bring her back. I notice that even as you're describing something so painful, there's a kind of quiet, almost rushed quality to the way you're sharing it, like you're moving through the words quickly to get past them. I'm wondering if part of you is working hard to hold something at a distance right now — and if so, we don't have to rush anywhere; we can just sit with whatever's here.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, maybe you're right that I'm rushing through it. I think if I slow down too much I'll just start crying and then feel embarrassed about it, which sounds ridiculous to say out loud. It's like I've been telling myself I should be further along by now, and everyone at these family things seems fine, so why am I still stuck here feeling like this?
therapist: It doesn't sound ridiculous at all — it sounds like you've been carrying a quiet rule that grief should follow a certain timeline, and when you don't meet it, you add shame on top of the pain you're already feeling. And comparing your insides to everyone else's outsides at those gatherings is such a hard trap to fall into, because you can't actually see what they're holding privately. I'm curious — where do you think that "should be over it by now" message first came from for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I think it probably comes from my family itself — we're not really people who dwell on things, you know? My dad especially, he's always been the type to just push through and get on with it, and I guess I absorbed that somewhere along the way. But hearing you say I'm comparing my insides to their outsides... I don't know, that's kind of stopping me, because I genuinely assumed they were all just doing better than me.
therapist: It sounds like that realization just landed somewhere real for you — that maybe your family's "push through" style taught you to measure your grief against a standard that doesn't leave much room for being human. And it's worth wondering whether your dad and the others at those gatherings might also be carrying more than they're showing, quietly following the same unspoken rule you inherited. What do you think it might feel like to give yourself even a little of the permission you'd probably offer someone else in your situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's a nice idea in theory, but honestly I don't really know how to do that — like, what does giving myself permission even look like in practice? I think if I tried to just tell myself "it's okay to still be sad," it would feel hollow, like I'm just saying words at myself. And part of me worries that if I actually let myself feel it fully, especially at one of those family gatherings, I'll just fall apart completely and that feels terrifying.
therapist: That fear of falling apart completely makes a lot of sense, especially when you've grown up in a family where holding it together is the unspoken expectation — but I'd gently push back on the idea that feeling it fully means losing control entirely. Permission doesn't have to mean opening a floodgate all at once; it might start with something much smaller, like letting yourself feel sad for just a few minutes in a private moment, rather than at the family table. What do you think the smallest, safest version of that might look like for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe something like sitting in my car for a few minutes before I go inside, or after I leave... I could see that being possible, I guess. But I'm a little skeptical of myself here, because I've tried things like that before and I just end up scrolling my phone to distract myself instead of actually feeling anything. I'm not sure I know how to just sit with something without immediately running away from it.
therapist: The fact that you already know your own pattern — reaching for the phone the moment things get uncomfortable — is actually really important self-awareness, and it tells me the avoidance isn't laziness, it's more like a well-practiced reflex to protect yourself from something that feels overwhelming. Sitting with emotion is genuinely a skill, and it makes sense it would feel unfamiliar if you grew up in a family where "push through" was the only tool in the box. I'm wondering — when you imagine putting the phone down and just sitting there, what is it you're most afraid you'd actually feel?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what I'm most afraid of is just how much I actually miss her — like, really miss her, not in a vague way but in this specific, sharp way that she's just not going to be there anymore at any of these gatherings, ever again. And I guess I'm scared that if I let myself feel that fully, it'll also come with this guilt I've been pushing down, because the last time I saw her I was distracted and didn't really talk to her properly. That's the part I really don't want to sit with.
therapist: What you just named — that sharp, specific missing of her, and the guilt underneath it — that feels like the real heart of what you've been carrying, and it takes real courage to say it out loud. That last visit is something so many grieving people hold onto, this one moment that becomes weighted with everything unsaid, but I'd gently ask you to consider whether the distracted, imperfect version of you that day was any less someone who loved her deeply. What do you think she would have made of that visit, if you could see it through her eyes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Honestly, she probably wouldn't have even noticed I was distracted — she was just happy when anyone showed up, that was always enough for her. But knowing that in my head and actually believing it feel like completely different things, and I'm worried you're going to tell me to just remind myself of that whenever the guilt comes up, because I don't think it'll work that way for me. It's like the guilt has its own logic that doesn't really respond to reasoning.
therapist: You're absolutely right that guilt doesn't operate like a logical argument you can just win — it lives somewhere deeper than that, and simply reminding yourself of the truth rarely touches it. What you just said about her, though — that anyone showing up was enough, that she was just happy you were there — that didn't sound like something you're indifferent to, and I noticed something shift in your voice as you said it, like it carries real weight for you. I wonder if the work isn't about convincing yourself with logic, but about finding ways to actually *feel* her acceptance of you as real — and I'm curious whether there are other memories of her that carry that same sense of being enough in her eyes.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: There are actually a lot of memories like that — she used to save newspaper clippings about things she thought I'd find interesting, even when I was an adult, just because she was thinking of me. And yeah, something about saying that out loud does feel different from the logical stuff, more like it lands somewhere. I'm just not sure how to hold onto that feeling, because it's there for a second and then the guilt kind of rushes back in and crowds it out.
therapist: Those newspaper clippings are such a tender image — she was thinking of you in quiet, consistent ways that had nothing to do with any single visit, and that's actually a portrait of how she held you in her mind. What you're describing, where the warmth lands for a moment and then guilt rushes in to crowd it out, is really common in grief, and it might help to think of those memories not as something to hold onto tightly, but as something you can return to — like you found a door today, and you can come back to it. I'm wondering if this week, before or after one of those gatherings, you might let yourself sit with just that one image of her saving those clippings, and notice what it feels like to be someone she thought of that way.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of it being a door I can come back to rather than something I have to grip onto — that framing actually feels less pressured somehow. But I'm a little worried that if I try to do this deliberately, like as a planned thing before a gathering, it'll feel forced and the guilt will just hijack it anyway. I guess I'm also not sure I deserve to feel comforted by those memories yet, which maybe tells me something about how deep this guilt actually goes.
therapist: That last thing you said — that you're not sure you *deserve* to feel comforted yet — that's such an important thing to notice, because it suggests the guilt has quietly appointed itself as a kind of gatekeeper to your own healing. And I want to sit with that for a moment, because deserving comfort isn't something you earn by suffering enough first — grief isn't a debt you pay off. I'm curious, if a close friend came to you carrying the exact same guilt about their grandmother, would you tell them they had to earn the right to feel comforted by good memories first?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: No, of course I wouldn't say that to a friend — I'd probably be frustrated if they even suggested they had to earn it. But it's so much easier to extend that to someone else than to myself, and I think part of me feels like the rules are just different when it's me, like I'm a special case where the guilt is actually justified. I don't fully know how to argue my way out of that belief even when I can see the double standard right in front of me.
therapist: The fact that you can see the double standard so clearly but still can't quite let it apply to you tells me this isn't really a thinking problem — it's something older and more lodged than that, and that's actually important, because it means arguing your way out of it probably isn't the path forward. I notice there's something almost urgent in the way you're talking about this right now, like you're working very hard to figure it out and solve it in this moment. I'm wondering what it would feel like to just let that "I'm a special case" belief sit there without trying to defeat it today — to simply notice it with a little curiosity, the way you might look at something through a window, rather than feeling like you have to dismantle it right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
